## Jeremiah 23 – Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Structure Overview

The chapter has three main sections:
- **vv. 1–8**: Judgment on unfaithful shepherds (civil rulers) and promise of the Righteous Branch
- **vv. 9–32**: Denunciation of false prophets
- **vv. 33–40**: The wordplay on "burden" (*massa*)

---

### v. 1 — "Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of My pasture!"

**Traditional Reading:** The "shepherds" (*pastors* in older translations) are primarily the **civil rulers** — the kings and magistrates of Judah. Ellicott notes that "pastors" here means "the civil rulers, not the prophets or the priests," like "shepherds of the people" in Greek poets. Gill agrees: "the civil rulers and magistrates, kings and princes of the land of Israel; since ecclesiastical rulers, the priests and prophets, are mentioned as distinct from them in Jeremiah 23:9." David Guzik (Enduring Word) says "in those days, kings and other leaders were often called shepherds; the term didn't necessarily have a spiritual context," though he adds modern application to spiritual leaders. Precept Austin notes "the 'shepherds' are the spiritual leaders of Israel, kings, priests, and prophets, entrusted with the care of God's flock."

The "woe" is a formal declaration of coming judgment. The charge is twofold: **destroying** (harming the flock) and **scattering** (failing to keep them together). Ellicott observes the parallel with Ezekiel 34, suggesting "either direct communication between the two writers, or of traditional lines of thought common to the two priest-prophets."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/23.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/23.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-23/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-23-commentary

### v. 2 — "You have scattered My flock… I will attend to you for the evil of your deeds"

The Hebrew verb *paqad* ("attend" / "visit") is used twice with a deliberate double meaning. Precept Austin explains: "The term 'attended' is the translation of *paqad* which can be rendered 'pay attention to,' 'look after,' … or 'call into account.' This latter meaning seems to be the idea in the second usage." The shepherds did not "visit" (care for) the flock, so God will "visit" (punish) them.

Ellicott adds that the charge was "true literally as well as spiritually. The dispersion of the people in Egypt, Assyria, and Chaldæa was the result of the neglect, the tyranny, the feebleness of their rulers. They had been led, not as the Eastern shepherd leads (John 10:4-5), but 'driven' — not to the fold, but 'away' into far lands."

Gill notes that these sheep "are called his sheep, and the sheep of his pasture; having made a covenant with their fathers, and provided a good pasture for them."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/23.htm
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-23-commentary
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/23.htm

### v. 3 — "I Myself will gather the remnant of My flock from all the lands"

God Himself takes over the shepherd's role. Precept Austin sees this pointing to **future, unfulfilled prophecy**: "This is not a reference to the return from captivity under Ezra, Nehemiah, and Zerubbabel … Rather these verses point toward unfulfilled prophecy — His return in glory to execute justice and judgment." Enduring Word takes a both/and approach: "The modern-day miracle of Israel becoming an independent nation once again, after some 2500 years, is an initial fulfillment … We say initial, because Israel is definitely gathered back to the land, but presently in unbelief."

Gill notes God takes responsibility for the scattering: "this, which is before charged upon the pastors, is taken by the Lord to himself; because this was not only permitted by him … but was inflicted by him as a punishment." Yet mercy prevails: He will gather "the remnant." Gill also sees a spiritual application: "an emblem of the Lord's bringing his chosen remnant, whether Jews or Gentiles, into a good fold … to a Gospel church state."

Ellicott: "There was hope, as in Isaiah 1:9; Isaiah 6:13, for the 'remnant' of the people, though the sentence on their rulers, as such, was final and irreversible."

- https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-23-commentary
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-23/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/23.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/23.htm

### v. 4 — "I will raise up shepherds over them who will tend them"

**Key theological point — relates shepherds to Messiah:** The plural "shepherds" has been understood in multiple ways:

- **Near-term fulfillment**: Gill sees Zerubbabel, Ezra, Nehemiah and others after the exile; also "Christian kings and princes" and "the apostles of Christ" (citing Jerome) and Gospel ministers. "They shall fear no more, nor be dismayed" — Gill notes this points beyond the return, since under Sanballat, Tobiah, the Greeks and Romans the Jews did fear. Thus "even to the times of Christ, and the Gospel dispensation."

- **Future eschatological**: Precept Austin sees v.4 as part of a future prophecy: "He will provide worthy shepherds to lead them (v. 4) and will raise up Jesus Christ, the Righteous Branch, the Messiah King (v. 5)."

- Ellicott notes the plural is "noticeable, as in Jeremiah 3:15, as not limiting the prophecy to the Christ who is yet the 'chief Shepherd' (1 Peter 5:4)." He sees a break from the hereditary Davidic succession, giving power to those like Ezra, Nehemiah, and the Maccabees "who had the capacity for ruling well."

The phrase "nor will any go missing" (BSB) / "neither shall they be lacking" (KJV) is seen by Ellicott as "care extending even to every individual member was the true ideal of the Shepherd's work (John 10:3; John 17:12)."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/23.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/23.htm
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-23-commentary

---

### v. 5 — "Behold, the days are coming… I will raise up for David a righteous Branch"

**This is one of the great Messianic prophecies.** All traditional interpreters across traditions agree it refers to the Messiah. Here are the key interpretive points:

**"Branch" (Hebrew *tsemach*):** Ellicott explains this is "a 'sprout' or 'scion,' springing up from the root even after the tree had been cut down (Isaiah 6:13), and not a branch growing from the trunk." The Davidic dynasty appeared cut down (see Jeremiah 22:30 on Jeconiah). Enduring Word: "It seemed as if the royal line of David was cut down like a tree and only a stump remained. Yet God would take that stump and bring forth a green shoot, a Branch."

**Calvin (Reformed)** emphasizes that this must refer to one individual King, not David's posterity in general: "The Jews, in order to obscure this prophecy, will have this to be applied to all the descendants of David … But such a thing cannot certainly be gathered from the words of the Prophet; for he does not speak here of many kings, but of one only." He adds that the prophets always set Christ before the people because "without Christ God cannot be a Father and a Savior to men."

**Precept Austin** notes that the Targum Jonathan (early Jewish paraphrase) explicitly reads: "Behold, the days are coming … and I will raise up to David a righteous **Messiah**." The Babylonian Talmud (Sanhedrin 98b) also ties "Branch" to the Messiah.

**The King's character:** He will "reign wisely" (or "act prudently" / "prosper"). Gill notes the Hebrew verb *sakal* can mean both "deal prudently" and "prosper" — as in Isaiah 52:13 of the Suffering Servant. Calvin: "the Prophet seems here to speak of right judgment rather than of success … Christ would be endued with the spirit of wisdom as well as of uprightness and equity."

Enduring Word notes: "A King shall reign: 'Moreover, he will reign as a true king, not as a puppet like Zedekiah and his immediate predecessors' (Feinberg)."

- https://ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol19/htm/vi.iii.htm (excerpts obtained via search)
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-23-commentary
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/23.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/23.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-23/

---

### v. 6 — "The LORD Our Righteousness" (Yahweh Tsidkenu)

**This is the crown of the chapter and a major point of theological richness.** The name in Hebrew is just two words: *Yahweh Tsidkenu*.

**Traditional Protestant understanding (imputed righteousness):**

- Gill (Baptist/Puritan): "because he is the author of righteousness to his people, and is only so … the Son of God only is; who is become so by his obedience to the law, and by bearing the penalty of it." Gill emphasizes that this righteousness "becomes 'ours' … through the imputation of it to us by the Father, and in virtue of our union to Christ."

- Calvin (Reformed): "Christ's righteousness … is ours, because Christ is righteous not for himself, but possesses a righteousness which he communicates to us … If, then, we desire to have God as our righteousness, we must seek Christ." He ties it to 1 Corinthians 1:30: Christ "made to us righteousness."

- Enduring Word (Pentecostal/charismatic): "Jesus is the Lord Our Righteousness: Righteousness is something positive. The work of Jesus in His people is not only to clean the stain of sin. The perfect obedience and righteousness of Jesus is ours in Him." Guzik also quotes Luther: "You, Sir Satan, your menaces and terrors trouble me not. For why? There is one whose name is called the Lord our righteousness, on whom I believe."

- Kretzmann (Lutheran): "No wonder, then, that His name would be called 'Jehovah Our Righteousness,' since, by virtue of His perfect atonement, all men may become partakers of the righteousness earned by Him for them."

- Garner-Howes (Baptist): notes the wordplay contrast with Zedekiah ("the Lord IS righteous") — the Messiah will be called "The Lord OUR righteousness."

**Deity of Messiah:** Enduring Word states "Yahweh Tsidkenu is strong evidence of the deity of the Messiah – He is Yahweh." The Targum reads "The Messiah of the righteous."

**Ellicott's nuanced reading (more cautious):** Ellicott notes that in Jeremiah 33:16 the same name is given to Jerusalem. He argues that we should not press the name as "the identification of the Messianic King with Jehovah" in a strict ontological sense. Rather, "That meaning would seem to be that the King, the righteous Branch, will look to Jehovah as giving and working righteousness." He still sees it as fulfilled in Christ who "answered to the name, not as being Himself one with Jehovah, though He was that, but as doing the Father's will, and so fulfilling all righteousness."

**Hastings' Great Text (modern/liberal):** Takes a more historical approach: "The ideal ruler whom Jeremiah foresees will govern his nation with wisdom and success; and under his gracious administration the Divinely imparted character of righteousness will be realized by the nation." It suggests Jeremiah may not have conceived of "justification, in the theological sense," but rather "ensuring, by his wise and just administration, the conditions under which righteousness of life might be maintained."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/23.htm
- https://ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol19/htm/vi.iii.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/23.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-23/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/jeremiah-23.html

### vv. 7–8 — "They will no longer say, 'As surely as the LORD lives, who brought the Israelites up out of Egypt'"

**A new Exodus.** The restoration from exile (and ultimately the Messianic salvation) will be so great that it eclipses the Exodus as the supreme act of God's deliverance. Gill: "which, though a wonderful deliverance, and never to be forgotten; yet not to be named with the redemption and salvation wrought out by Christ the Lord our righteousness."

Enduring Word: "Israel was created in the Exodus out of Egypt and they were restored in the gathering out of Babylon and the nations. God promised that the restoration of Israel would be greater than the creation of Israel. This connects to the principle that restored or redeemed man is greater than created or innocent man."

Gill sees a yet-future fulfillment for the ten tribes: "which has never been fulfilled as yet of the seed of the house of Israel, or of the ten tribes; but will be when all Israel shall be saved."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-23/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/23.htm

---

### v. 9 — "My heart is broken within me… I have become like a drunkard"

**Jeremiah's personal anguish.** The Hebrew text actually begins this section with a title: "Concerning the prophets:" — marking a new section. Jeremiah is not drunk with wine but overwhelmed with horror at the contrast between God's holy words and the false prophets' behavior. Ellicott: "the contrast between the words of Jehovah and His holiness on the one side, and the wickedness of priests and prophets on the other."

Gill: "his 'heart' within him was 'broken' with grief and sorrow, because of their false doctrines and wicked lives; and because of the mischief they did the people." The phrase "all my bones shake" is compared by Jarchi (Rashi) to "a fluttering motion as is made by the wings of a bird hovering over its nest."

Harrison (cited by Enduring Word): "Heart, as used here, denotes a profoundly disturbed mental rather than emotional state. His mind cannot grasp the way in which these prophets have chose to abuse their professional vocation."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/23.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/23.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-23/

---

### v. 10 — "The land is full of adulterers… because of the curse, the land mourns"

Ellicott insists "the words must be taken literally, and not of the spiritual adultery of the worship of other Gods. The false prophets and their followers were personally profligates, like those of 2 Peter 2:14." The "curse" (KJV "swearing") is better "the curse" — the divine curse on account of wickedness. The drought and dried pastures likely refer to the drought of Jeremiah 12:4 and 14:2.

Enduring Word: "The other prophets promised blessing and abundance, but the evidence was on Jeremiah's side. The heavy presence of sin in the land … and the curse upon the land itself proved that it was time to repent and not to relax."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/23.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-23/

---

### v. 11 — "Both prophet and priest are ungodly; even in My house I have found their wickedness"

The corruption reached into the Temple itself. Gill connects this to the times of Christ: "the Pharisees in Christ's time laid heavy burdens on others, but would not move them themselves; and, through a pretence of devotion, devoured widows' houses."

Ellicott: "It seems probable, from Jeremiah 32:34, that the sins of Ahaz and Manasseh had been repeated under Jehoiakim, and that the worship of other gods had been carried on side by side with that of Jehovah. With this, almost as its natural accompaniment, there may have been sins of another kind — shameless greed or yet more shameless profligacy — like those of the sons of Eli (1 Samuel 2:22)."

Enduring Word: "To be profane is the opposite of holiness. They weren't different from the idol worshipping people surrounding Judah."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/23.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-23/

---

### v. 12 — "Their path will become slick… driven away into the darkness"

The imagery of a slippery path in darkness recalls Psalm 35:5-6 and Isaiah 8:22. Ellicott: "The words and the thoughts flow in upon the prophet's mind from Isaiah 8:22; Psalm 35:5-6." The "year of their punishment" uses Jeremiah's characteristic word for the appointed time of divine chastisement (cf. Jer 8:12; 10:15; 11:23).

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/23.htm

---

### vv. 13–14 — Comparison: Samaria's prophets vs. Jerusalem's prophets

The prophets of Samaria (northern kingdom) "prophesied by Baal" — open idolatry, which is called "folly" (literally, "that which is unsavoury," Job 6:6). But Jerusalem's prophets are worse: they use the LORD's name while practicing adultery, lying, and strengthening evildoers. Ellicott: "The union of the claim to prophesy in the name of Jehovah with these flagrant breaches of His law was more hateful in the prophet's eyes even than the open recognition of Baal."

**"They are all like Sodom to Me":** Kidner (cited by Enduring Word) sees this as including sexual sin: "by their laxity (Jeremiah 23:14), whether practiced or preached, they are taking the shame out of sin (especially, it seems, sins of lust, both heterosexual, Jeremiah 23:14a, and homosexual, Jeremiah 23:14b; cf. Genesis 19:4-5)."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/23.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-23/

---

### v. 15 — "I will feed them wormwood and give them poisoned water to drink"

Wormwood is a bitter plant; "water of gall" (KJV) or "poisoned water" signifies bitter judgment. Feinberg (cited by Enduring Word): "Because they had poisoned the nation's spiritual springs, the Lord was to inflict drastic judgment on them." The term "profaneness" (KJV) / "ungodliness" (BSB) is the Hebrew *chanuppah*, which means hypocrisy or pollution. Ellicott notes it comes from a root meaning "veiling" — simulated holiness that desecrates.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-23/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/23.htm

---

### vv. 16–17 — "Do not listen to the words of the prophets… They keep saying… 'You will have peace'"

**The hallmark of false prophecy:** promising peace to the unrepentant. Enduring Word: "They could not or would not rebuke those who lived according to the dictates of his own heart. The failure or inability to confront evil is a mark of bad or corrupt leadership." Guzik notes the contrast: "His [Jeremiah's] main message was repent; their main message was relax."

Ellicott: "This was then, as always, the crucial test between the true prophet and the false. The one roused the conscience, caused pain and anger by his reproofs; the other soothed and quieted men with a false assurance." The Hebrew verb used for "The LORD has said" (v.17) is not the standard prophetic formula — "The prophet seems to indicate in this way that those whom he condemns placed the Divine message on a level with a man's every-day utterance."

Bridgeway: "The false prophets speak not God's words but their own. They encourage the people to do as they please, assuring them that God will not punish them."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-23/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/23.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/jeremiah-23.html

---

### v. 18 — "Which of them has stood in the council of the LORD?"

The "council" (Hebrew *sod*) is God's intimate assembly — like a king's privy council where secret plans are shared. Ellicott: "Could any of the false prophets say that they had thus been called as into the privy council of Jehovah? (Comp. Amos 3:7; 1 Kings 22:19-23.)" Bridgeway: "The reason the false prophets do not understand God's wrath is that they do not understand God. Their minds have never been taught by him."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/23.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/jeremiah-23.html

---

### vv. 19–20 — "The storm of the LORD has gone out with fury… a whirlwind"

The judgment is pictured as a violent, whirling tempest. Ellicott: the word is "properly more generic in its meaning ('tempest' in Isaiah 29:6), and gets its specific force here from the associated word … whirling." Clarke (cited by Enduring Word) identifies it as "the simoom: the hot pestilential wind blowing from the south."

v.20: "The anger of the LORD will not turn back until He has fully accomplished the purposes of His heart." This is the opposite of the false prophets' message. Those who followed "the dictates of his own heart" (v.17) will meet God's "thoughts of His heart." The phrase "in the days to come" (literally "the end of the days") points to a future time when all will become clear. Ellicott: "Men should look back on it in the 'latter days' … and should see that it had done its work both of chastisement and discipline."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/23.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-23/

---

### vv. 21–22 — "I did not send these prophets, yet they have run"

**The test of a true prophet:** Ellicott notes the image of messengers who "rush eagerly, as from the king's council-chamber, on their self-appointed mission, without waiting for the command of the Master." v.22 gives a practical test: if they had truly stood in God's council, they would have turned the people from evil, not confirmed them in it. Ellicott raises an honest objection — was Jeremiah himself "successful" by this measure? He answers: true teaching "at least stirs and rouses men from lethargy, even if it stirs them to antagonism. It is never satisfied with speaking smooth things."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/23.htm

---

### vv. 23–24 — "Am I only a God nearby… and not a God far away? … Do I not fill the heavens and the earth?"

**God's omnipresence and omniscience.** The false prophets acted as if God were a local deity who could be avoided. Ellicott: "The false prophets acted as if God were far away out of their sight (Psalm 10:11; Psalm 73:11; Psalm 94:7), not knowing or caring what men did." Precept Austin: "Yahweh is not a God near, a local man-made deity whose domain and wisdom are limited … He is omnipotent, omnipresent, and omniscient." Trapp (cited by Enduring Word): "Atheists are apt to think that because they see none, therefore none see them."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/23.htm
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-23-commentary
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-23/

---

### vv. 25–27 — "I have heard… 'I had a dream! I had a dream!'"

The false prophets claimed dreams as the source of their revelations. Deuteronomy 13:1-5 already provided a test for dreamers: does their message accord with God's revealed law? The problem was that these "dreams" were "the deceit of their own heart" (v.26). Enduring Word notes two possibilities: "Perhaps the lie was that they even had such a dream, or perhaps they really had a dream but it was not a true message from God."

v.27: Their goal was to make people forget God's name (His character), just as Baal worship had done earlier. Thompson (cited by Enduring Word): "Once men forgot the character of Yahweh they could be persuaded to accept all kinds of doctrines."

Ellicott notes that the misuse of dreams brought them into discredit, "of the disparagement of dreams, consequent on this abuse, we have a striking example in Ecclesiastes 5:3, and later still in Ecclesiasticus 34:1-7."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-23/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/23.htm

---

### vv. 28–29 — "What is straw compared to grain? … Is not My word like fire… and like a hammer that smashes a rock?"

**The supremacy of God's Word over spiritual phenomena.** v.28: Let the dreamer tell his dream as what it is — a dream. But let God's true word be spoken faithfully. The contrast "chaff to wheat" is stark: one is worthless, the other nourishes life. Ellicott: "What have they in common? What has one to do with the other?"

v.29: Two powerful images. **Fire**: the true prophetic word burns in the prophet (Jer 5:14; 20:9) and consumes evil and purifies good (cf. 1 Cor 3:12-13). **Hammer**: it shatters pride and stubbornness; "mighty to the pulling down of strongholds" (2 Cor 10:4). Ellicott: "the heart of him who hears it as it should be heard is broken and contrite."

Bridgeway: "The messages of the false prophets are like straw, whereas the messages of the true prophets are like wheat. They nourish what is good. At the same time they are like fire or a hammer, because they destroy what is worthless."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/23.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-23/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/jeremiah-23.html

---

### vv. 30–32 — "I am against the prophets who steal from one another words they attribute to Me"

**Three "I am against" declarations** expose three forms of false prophecy:

- **v.30 — Stealing words**: Plagiarizing each other's messages. Ellicott: "The oracles of the dreamers were patchworks of plagiarism … What we should call the 'clique' of false prophets went on repeating each other's phrases with a wearisome iteration." They also borrowed from true prophets' language. Coffman: a warning against "imitative, second-hand prophecy."

- **v.31 — Wagging their own tongues**: Using their own eloquence and declaring "The LORD declares it." Ellicott: "The scornful phrase indicates the absence of a true inspiration. These false prophets plan their schemes, and take their tongue as an instrument for carrying them into effect."

- **v.32 — False dreams and reckless lies**: Leading people astray. "They are of no benefit at all" — the ultimate uselessness of false prophecy.

Bridgeway: "False prophets only lie and deceive. They even take the words of the true prophets and misapply them in order to support their own ideas."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/23.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/jeremiah-23.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/jeremiah-23.html

---

### vv. 33–40 — The "Burden" Wordplay

This section is built on a pun in Hebrew: the word *massa* means both **"burden"** (a heavy load) and **"oracle"** (a prophetic revelation). The people, prophets, and priests were apparently mocking Jeremiah by asking, "What is the *massa* (burden/oracle) of the LORD?" — perhaps with a sneer implying that Jeremiah's message was a tiresome burden.

**God's response** (v.33): When they ask about the "burden," Jeremiah is to answer with a pun: "What burden? I will forsake you!" The Hebrew for "forsake" (*natash*) sounds like a play on *nasa* ("to lift up / carry away"). You ask about a burden? You yourselves are the burden, and I will throw you off.

**v.34–36**: God forbids the use of "the burden of the LORD" as a flippant formula. Bridgeway explains: "The false prophets misused the word 'burden', so that no matter what announcement they made, they claimed it to be a burden from God. For this reason God commands the true prophets, such as Jeremiah, not to use the word any more." Instead, people should use straightforward language: "What has the LORD answered?" or "What has the LORD spoken?"

Enduring Word (from the excerpt obtained): "This section is somewhat difficult because of a pun and wordplay in Hebrew. The key word is *massa* which meant both burden and oracle … Sometimes one sense of the word is intended, sometimes the other, and sometimes both."

**v.36**: "Each man's word becomes the burden" — by calling their own words God's oracle, they pervert God's words.

**v.39–40**: Severe judgment: God will "forget you" (a wordplay — *nashiti*, "I will forget," sounds like *massa*) and cast them out with "everlasting shame and perpetual humiliation."

Peake's Commentary (modern/critical): "When men scornfully ask about Yahweh's 'burden', the answer, playing on the term, shall be 'Ye are the burden' … If men persist in using this term 'burden' of Yahweh's oracles, he will 'take them up' … again with a play on words."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-23/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/jeremiah-23.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/jeremiah-23.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/jeremiah-23.html

## Denominational Distinctives Observed

**Reformed (Calvin):** Strong emphasis on the Messiah as the sole mediator and the imputation of His righteousness. Calvin explicitly rejects the Jewish interpretation that "Branch" refers to David's posterity collectively, insisting it is Christ alone. The name "Yahweh Tsidkenu" proves that righteousness is not in Christ merely for Himself but "communicated to us." (ccel.org/calvin)

**Lutheran (Kretzmann):** Emphasizes the atonement: "by virtue of His perfect atonement, all men may become partakers of the righteousness earned by Him for them." Also applies "Judah" and "Israel" spiritually to "the true spiritual Israel, the Church of Christ." (studylight.org Kretzmann)

**Baptist (Gill):** Strong on the particularity of the atonement — Christ is righteousness for "God's elect." Also emphasizes the yet-future restoration of the ten tribes ("which has never been fulfilled as yet … but will be when all Israel shall be saved"). Gill uniquely ties v.3 to John 10:16 (sheep "not of this fold"). (biblehub.com/gill)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word/Guzik):** Emphasizes the modern-day restoration of Israel as partial fulfillment; also gives strong practical application of testing prophetic words (1 Cor 14:29; 1 Thess 5:20-21; 1 John 4:1). Maintains the traditional Messianic reading of vv.5-6 while also seeing near-term fulfillments. (enduringword.com)

**Modern/Liberal Scholarship (Hastings, Peake):** Hastings suggests Jeremiah may not have intended the full theological sense of "justification" but rather "ensuring, by his wise and just administration, the conditions under which righteousness of life might be maintained." Peake treats the text with attention to source criticism (suggesting vv.19-20 are an interpolation from Jer 30:23f). (studylight.org Hastings, Peake)
